questions.stem: When a Group 1 metal reacts, how many electrons does its atom need to lose from its outer shell?

options.text: One, because Group 1 atoms have a single electron in their outermost shell
options.explanation: The single outer electron is all that stands between the atom and a full outer shell, so one loss completes the noble gas pattern.

options.text: Seven, to empty the outer shell completely
options.explanation: Emptying the shell is far harder than losing one electron; the atom loses the lone outer electron and the full shell beneath becomes the new outer shell.
options.misconception: counting valency of non-metals instead of Group 1 metals

options.text: It depends on the size of the atom
options.explanation: Every Group 1 atom carries one outer electron regardless of size; size affects how easily it is lost, not how many are lost.
options.misconception: atom size thought to set the electron count

options.text: Two, so that a 2+ ion forms like Group 2 metals
options.explanation: Group 1 metals sit one column left of the noble gases with one outer electron, so they form 1+ ions, not 2+ ions.
options.misconception: group number misread for ionic charge

questions.stem: What charge does the ion formed when a Group 1 metal reacts always carry?

options.text: A 1+ charge
options.explanation: Losing the single negatively charged outer electron leaves one more proton than electron, so the ion carries a single positive charge.

options.text: A 1- charge
options.explanation: A negative ion forms by gaining electrons; Group 1 atoms lose their outer electron instead, so the ion is positive.
options.misconception: gain and loss of electrons confused

options.text: No charge, because the atom keeps all its electrons
options.explanation: Reaction is only possible because the outer electron is lost; keeping every electron would leave a neutral atom with an incomplete shell.
options.misconception: ion formation not linked to electron loss

options.text: A charge that grows larger further down the group
options.explanation: Every alkali metal forms the same 1+ ion; what changes down the group is how easily that ion forms.
options.misconception: trend in reactivity mistaken for trend in charge

questions.stem: After a Group 1 atom loses its outer electron, why is the resulting ion stable?

options.text: The shell underneath is already full, so the ion has a noble gas configuration
options.explanation: Removing the lone outer electron promotes the complete shell below to the outside, matching the electron arrangement of a noble gas.

options.text: The ion has lost all of its electrons
options.explanation: Only the outer electron is lost; the filled inner shells remain, and it is their completeness that makes the ion stable.
options.misconception: ion assumed to be a bare nucleus

options.text: The ion gains extra protons to balance the charge
options.explanation: The proton count never changes during ordinary reactions; stability comes from the full outer shell, not from new protons.
options.misconception: nuclear change assumed during ion formation

options.text: Stability comes from the ion being smaller than the atom
options.explanation: The 1+ ion is indeed smaller, but that is a consequence of losing a shell; the stability itself comes from the full outer shell.
options.misconception: size change mistaken for the cause of stability

questions.stem: Which statement correctly states the reactivity trend of the alkali metals?

options.text: Reactivity increases as you go down Group 1
options.explanation: Lithium, then sodium, then potassium react more and more vigorously, so reactivity climbs on descending the group.

options.text: Reactivity decreases as you go down Group 1
options.explanation: This is the Group 7 pattern; Group 1 behaves in the opposite way because it loses rather than gains electrons.
options.misconception: Group 7 trend copied onto Group 1

options.text: All Group 1 metals are equally reactive
options.explanation: The shared one-outer-electron pattern makes their reactions similar in type, but the vigour clearly changes down the group.
options.misconception: similarity of reaction type read as equal vigour

options.text: Reactivity depends only on how much metal is used
options.explanation: The trend is fixed by electron arrangement; the amount of metal changes how long a reaction lasts, not its position in the trend.
options.misconception: quantity confused with intrinsic reactivity

questions.stem: Why do all the alkali metals have similar chemical reactions?

options.text: They each have one electron in their outermost shell
options.explanation: Reactions are governed by outer-shell electrons, and sharing the single-outer-electron pattern gives the group its common chemistry.

options.text: They all have the same number of electron shells
options.explanation: The shell count rises down the group; it is the outer-shell count of one that the metals share.
options.misconception: total shells confused with outer electrons

options.text: They all have the same number of protons
options.explanation: Each element has its own proton count; identical protons would make them the same element, not a group.
options.misconception: identity of the element confused with its reactions

options.text: They all form 2+ ions when they react
options.explanation: Each alkali metal forms a 1+ ion; the shared ion charge follows from the shared outer-electron count.
options.misconception: ion charge misremembered

questions.stem: State the electron loss and the ion formed when a Group 1 metal takes part in a reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: It needs to lose only the single electron in its outer shell, forming a 1+ ion with a full outer shell.

questions.stem: Why is the ion formed by a reacting Group 1 metal atom stable?
questions.modelAnswer: The filled shell underneath becomes the outermost shell, so the ion gains a noble gas configuration.

questions.stem: Account for the shared reaction pattern of the alkali metals using the one-outer-electron structure.
questions.modelAnswer: They all share the one-outer-electron pattern: each atom needs to lose only its single outer electron to reach a noble gas configuration, so every alkali metal reacts in the same way.

questions.stem: An unseen metal X sits directly below potassium in Group 1. Predict how many electrons one atom of X loses and whether X reacts more or less vigorously than potassium, giving the trend law you used.
questions.modelAnswer: One electron: like every Group 1 atom, X loses its single outer electron to form a 1+ ion. X reacts more vigorously than potassium, because reactivity increases down the group.

questions.stem: How does the number of occupied electron shells change between lithium, sodium and potassium?

options.text: It rises by one shell at each successive element
options.explanation: Lithium has two shells, sodium three and potassium four, so each step down the group adds one complete shell.

options.text: It stays the same, because all Group 1 atoms look alike
options.explanation: The atoms share one outer electron but not the same shell count; the growing size down the group is caused by the added shells.
options.misconception: group similarity read as identical structure

options.text: It falls by one shell at each successive element
options.explanation: Atoms get larger, not smaller, down the group, because each element occupies a further period with an extra shell.
options.misconception: trend direction reversed

options.text: It doubles at each successive element
options.explanation: Shell counts grow one at a time down the group; doubling would give atom sizes far beyond anything observed.
options.misconception: exaggerated growth pattern invented

questions.stem: Why is the outer electron of potassium lost more easily than that of sodium?

options.text: It sits further from the nucleus, so the attraction it feels is weaker
options.explanation: Potassium's extra shell places its outer electron further out, and electrostatic attraction weakens with distance, so the electron is lost more easily.

options.text: Potassium's nucleus has a smaller positive charge
options.explanation: Potassium actually has more protons than sodium; the easier loss comes from the greater distance, not a weaker nuclear charge.
options.misconception: proton count misread down the group

options.text: Potassium has fewer electron shells than sodium
options.explanation: Potassium has one more shell than sodium, which is exactly why its outer electron sits further out.
options.misconception: shell order inverted

options.text: Potassium atoms weigh less, so they react faster
options.explanation: Potassium atoms are heavier than sodium atoms; reactivity follows electron distance, not atomic mass.
options.misconception: mass-based reasoning about reactivity

questions.stem: What happens to the energy needed to remove the outer electron as you go down Group 1?

options.text: It decreases, because the weaker attraction is easier to overcome
options.explanation: With the outer electron further from the nucleus, less energy is needed to overcome the attraction, so removal becomes easier.

options.text: It increases, because the atoms are heavier
options.explanation: Mass does not set the removal energy; the distance of the outer electron from the nucleus does.
options.misconception: mass substituted for attraction

options.text: It stays constant across the group
options.explanation: A constant removal energy would give equal reactivity, but the vigour of the reactions clearly rises down the group.
options.misconception: flat trend assumed

options.text: It first rises and then falls
options.explanation: The trend is a steady fall down the group; each added shell weakens the hold on the outer electron a little more.
options.misconception: non-monotonic trend invented

questions.stem: A student claims sodium is more reactive than potassium because sodium is higher in the group. What is the correct verdict?

options.text: Wrong: potassium is lower in Group 1, so its outer electron is lost more easily and it is more reactive
options.explanation: Reactivity increases down Group 1, so potassium, sitting below sodium, reacts more vigorously.

options.text: Correct: higher placement in the group always means greater reactivity
options.explanation: That reading inverts the Group 1 trend; higher placement here means fewer shells and a more strongly held outer electron.
options.misconception: trend direction misapplied

options.text: Both metals are equally reactive, so the claim does not matter
options.explanation: The reactions are similar in type but clearly different in vigour, with potassium reacting violently where sodium reacts quickly.
options.misconception: equal reactivity assumed

options.text: The claim cannot be judged without measuring reaction rates
options.explanation: The periodic table position alone settles the ordering, because reactivity follows the electron arrangement down the group.
options.misconception: empirical testing demanded where the trend decides

questions.stem: In an exam answer, which chain of reasoning best explains the increasing reactivity down Group 1?

options.text: More shells, greater distance from the nucleus, weaker attraction, easier electron loss
options.explanation: This chain runs from the electron arrangement to the energy outcome, which is exactly what the specification asks you to explain.

options.text: More protons, stronger attraction, harder electron loss
options.explanation: That chain would predict falling reactivity; the added shells outpace the added charge, so distance dominates the outcome.
options.misconception: nuclear charge reasoning used instead of distance

options.text: Larger atoms, more collisions, faster reactions
options.explanation: Collision frequency is about reacting mixtures, not about how easily a single atom loses its outer electron.
options.misconception: collision theory misapplied to electron loss

options.text: Lower melting points, so the metals melt first and react faster
options.explanation: Melting points do fall down the group, but they are not the cause of the reactivity trend; electron distance is.
options.misconception: physical property mistaken for the cause

questions.stem: State the shell-count step made at each element on descending from lithium through sodium to potassium.
questions.modelAnswer: The number of occupied shells rises by one at each element going down the group.

questions.stem: What happens to the amount of energy needed to remove the outer electron on descending Group 1?
questions.modelAnswer: Less energy is needed to overcome the weaker attraction, so the outer electron is lost more easily down the group.

questions.stem: Explain, in terms of distance and attraction, why potassium's outer electron is lost more easily than sodium's.
questions.modelAnswer: The extra shell places potassium's outermost electron further away from the nucleus; the greater distance weakens the pull between the nucleus and that electron, so less energy is needed to remove it and it is lost more easily.

questions.stem: Rubidium sits between potassium and caesium in Group 1. Predict whether rubidium's outer electron is lost more or less easily than potassium's, and state the reactivity consequence, using the shell-distance chain.
questions.modelAnswer: Rubidium has one more occupied shell than potassium, so its outer electron sits further from the nucleus, the attraction is weaker and the electron is lost more easily; rubidium is therefore more reactive than potassium.
